# Freelance Deposit & Milestone Payment Kit

Stop starting work for free and stop chasing one big invoice at the end.
This kit helps you split any project into a deposit plus milestone payments,
explain it to clients without awkwardness, and keep track of what's due.

## What's inside

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `payment-structures.md` | Pick the right structure for the project size, with a fully worked example |
| `milestone-schedule.csv` | Tracker for deposits and milestone invoices (filled example rows) |
| `client-emails.md` | Eight ready-to-edit emails: proposing the schedule, deposit request, milestone invoices, a late milestone, pausing work |
| `payment-terms-wording.md` | Plain-English wording for proposals and agreements |
| `kickoff-checklist.md` | What to confirm before you start any work |
| `objection-replies.md` | Calm answers to "Can we pay at the end?" and five other pushbacks |

## How to use it (20 minutes)

1. Open `payment-structures.md`, find your project size, and pick a structure.
2. Copy the example rows in `milestone-schedule.csv`, replace them with your
   project, and check the percentages add up to 100.
3. Paste the matching wording from `payment-terms-wording.md` into your proposal.
4. Send email 1 from `client-emails.md` with the proposal, then email 2 for the deposit.
5. Don't start work until the deposit has cleared. Use `kickoff-checklist.md`.

## Opening the tracker
`milestone-schedule.csv` opens in Excel, Google Sheets (File > Import) or Numbers.
The `Days late` column is left blank on purpose: add a formula such as
`=IF(AND(J2="",TODAY()>H2),TODAY()-H2,"")` once it's in your spreadsheet.

## A note
This kit gives general business guidance and example wording, not legal or
tax advice. Payment rules differ by country and contract, so check anything
important with a qualified professional where you work.
files.payment-structures.md:
# Choosing a Payment Structure

The goal is simple: never be owed more than you can afford to lose. A deposit
covers you if the client disappears early; milestones keep the amount at risk
small as the work goes on.

## Quick picker

| Project value | Length | Suggested structure |
|---|---|---|
| Under $1,000 | Under 2 weeks | 100% up front, or 50% deposit / 50% on delivery |
| $1,000 – $5,000 | 2–6 weeks | 50% deposit / 50% on delivery, or 40 / 30 / 30 |
| $5,000 – $20,000 | 1–3 months | 30% deposit, then 3 milestones (e.g. 30 / 25 / 25 / 20) |
| Over $20,000 | 3+ months | 20–25% deposit, then monthly or per-phase invoices |
| Ongoing work | Open-ended | Monthly in advance (see a retainer setup) |

Rules of thumb:

- **Tie milestones to things the client can see**: "homepage design approved",
  not "50% of hours done". Visible milestones are easier to invoice and harder to dispute.
- **Keep the final payment smaller than the deposit** where you can. The last
  payment is the one most likely to drift.
- **Release final files on final payment.** Share previews, staging links or
  watermarked drafts before then.
- **Set a due date on every milestone invoice** (7 or 14 days is common) and
  say what happens if it's missed (work pauses).
- **Approval deadlines matter too.** If milestone payment depends on approval,
  add "approved, or 5 business days after delivery with no change requests".

## Worked example: website redesign, $8,400

A designer quotes $8,400 for a 10-week site redesign.

| # | Milestone | Trigger | % | Amount | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Deposit | Signed agreement | 30% | $2,520 | Before work starts |
| 1 | Design direction approved | Moodboard + homepage concept approved | 25% | $2,100 | 7 days after invoice |
| 2 | All page designs approved | Final designs signed off | 25% | $2,100 | 7 days after invoice |
| 3 | Launch | Site live, files handed over | 20% | $1,680 | On delivery, before file handover |
| | **Total** | | **100%** | **$8,400** | |

Check the maths: 2,520 + 2,100 + 2,100 + 1,680 = 8,400.

What this protects: at no point is the designer owed more than one milestone
($2,100) of finished, unpaid work. Without milestones, they could have been owed
the whole $8,400 at the end.

## Working out your own

1. Write down 3–5 moments the client will clearly see progress.
2. Put the deposit first (20–50% depending on size and how well you know them).
3. Spread the rest over the milestones, roughly in line with effort.
4. Round to whole currency amounts and make sure the total equals the quote.
5. Put the schedule in the proposal and the agreement, word for word the same.

## New or risky clients

Ask for a larger deposit (50%) or full payment up front when: the client is new
and unreferred, the budget is small, the timeline is rushed, or they have
reservations about paying on time. You can relax it on the second project.

files.client-emails.md:
# Client Emails

Replace anything in [brackets]. Keep them short; the schedule itself lives in
your proposal or agreement.

---

## 1. Introducing the payment schedule (with the proposal)

**Subject:** Proposal for [project] + how payment works

Hi [Name],

Attached is the proposal for [project]. The total is [amount], split into
[number] payments so neither of us carries too much at once:

- [30%] deposit ([amount]) to book the start date
- [25%] when [milestone 1] is approved
- [25%] when [milestone 2] is approved
- [20%] at launch, before final file handover

Each invoice is due within [7] days. Happy to talk through any of it.

[Your name]

---

## 2. Deposit invoice

**Subject:** Deposit invoice – [project] (starts [date])

Hi [Name],

Thanks for signing. Here's the deposit invoice for [amount] ([invoice number]).
Once it clears I'll lock in [start date] and send the kickoff questions.

Payment options are on the invoice. Let me know if your team needs anything
else to process it (a PO number, supplier form, etc.).

[Your name]

---

## 3. Deposit reminder before the start date

**Subject:** Quick check – deposit for [project]

Hi [Name],

Just checking the deposit invoice ([invoice number], [amount]) reached the right
person. We're set to start on [date]; I'll need it cleared by [date] to keep
that slot. If anything's holding it up, tell me and we'll sort it out.

[Your name]

---

## 4. Milestone reached + invoice

**Subject:** [Milestone] approved – invoice [number]

Hi [Name],

Great to have [milestone] signed off. As per our schedule, here's the invoice
for [amount], due [date]. Next up: [next milestone], which I expect to share by [date].

[Your name]

---

## 5. Approval is overdue (milestone tied to sign-off)

**Subject:** [Milestone] – feedback by [date]?

Hi [Name],

I shared [deliverable] on [date]. Could you send feedback or approval by [date]?
Per our agreement, if I don't hear back by then I'll treat it as approved and
send the milestone invoice, so the project keeps moving.

[Your name]

---

## 6. Milestone invoice is late (friendly)

**Subject:** Invoice [number] – due [date]

Hi [Name],

A quick reminder that invoice [number] for [amount] was due on [date]. Could
you let me know when to expect payment? I've reattached it in case it got buried.

[Your name]

---

## 7. Pausing work until payment

**Subject:** Pausing [project] until invoice [number] is paid

Hi [Name],

Invoice [number] ([amount]) is now [X] days overdue. As set out in our agreement,
I'm pausing work on [project] from [date] until it's paid. I'll pick up again
as soon as it clears; the delivery dates will move by the length of the pause.

If there's a problem on your side, reply and let's find a way through it.

[Your name]

---

## 8. Final payment and handover

**Subject:** [Project] is live – final invoice and handover

Hi [Name],

[Project] is live. Here's the final invoice ([number], [amount]). As soon as it's
paid I'll send the full handover: [source files / logins / documentation].
Thank you, it's been a great project.

[Your name]

# Payment Terms Wording

Example wording to adapt for proposals and agreements. This is general
information, not legal advice; if a project is large or the rules where you or
your client work are unusual, have a professional review your terms.

## Deposit

> A non-refundable deposit of [30]% ([amount]) is due on signing. Work, and the
> reserved start date, begin once the deposit has cleared.

If you'd rather it be refundable in some cases, say exactly when:

> The deposit is refundable in full if the client cancels at least [14] days
> before the start date. After that, it covers time reserved and is non-refundable.

Check the rules where you work: some places limit what can be kept as non-refundable.

## Milestone payments

> The remaining balance is paid in instalments at the milestones below. Each
> milestone invoice is due within [7] days of issue.
>
> 1. [Milestone 1] – [25]% ([amount])
> 2. [Milestone 2] – [25]% ([amount])
> 3. [Final delivery] – [20]% ([amount])

## Deemed approval

> If the client does not request changes within [5] business days of a
> milestone delivery, the milestone is treated as approved and invoiced.

## Pausing work

> If an invoice is more than [7] days overdue, the freelancer may pause work
> until it is paid. Deadlines move by the length of any pause.

## Ownership and final files

> Ownership of final deliverables and source files transfers to the client
> once all invoices have been paid in full.

## Cancellation mid-project

> If the project is cancelled after work begins, the client pays for all
> completed milestones plus work done on the current milestone, at [rate] or
> [percent]% of that milestone, whichever is lower.

## Late fees (optional)

> Overdue invoices may incur a late fee of [rate] per [month], where permitted by law.

Many freelancers leave this out and rely on pausing work instead. If you
include it, check what's allowed in your country or state.
files.kickoff-checklist.md:
# Before You Start Work: Kickoff Checklist

Tick every line before you open the project file.

## Agreement
- [ ] Proposal or agreement signed by someone with authority to sign
- [ ] Payment schedule is the same in the proposal, agreement and tracker
- [ ] Milestones are things the client can see and approve
- [ ] Invoice due dates (e.g. 7 or 14 days) are written down
- [ ] Approval deadline / deemed approval wording included
- [ ] What happens if payment is late (work pauses) is written down
- [ ] Final files released on final payment is written down

## Money
- [ ] Deposit invoice sent
- [ ] Deposit has **cleared** (not just "it's been sent")
- [ ] You know who pays invoices (name + email) and how (bank transfer, card, platform)
- [ ] Any PO number, supplier form or billing address the client needs is on the invoice
- [ ] Tracker updated with all milestone rows and amounts

## Project
- [ ] Start date confirmed
- [ ] First milestone date shared with the client
- [ ] Who gives feedback and approves milestones is named
- [ ] Kickoff call or questions sent

## Red flags (raise the deposit or pause before starting)
- Client asks you to start "while finance sorts the deposit"
- The person signing isn't the person paying, and you haven't met the payer
- Scope is still vague, but the deadline is fixed
- Pushback on every payment term, not just one
files.objection-replies.md:
# Replies to Common Pushback

Stay friendly and specific. You're explaining how you work, not asking permission.

**"Can we just pay everything at the end?"**
> I split payments on every project so neither side carries too much risk at
> once. You only pay for each stage once you've seen and approved it.

**"Our policy is net 30/60 – we can't pay a deposit."**
> Understood. Could we invoice the deposit now so it lands in your next payment
> run, and set the start date to match? Alternatively I can start once it's
> approved for payment with a PO number. *(Then adjust the start date.)*

**"Can you start now? The deposit will come next week."**
> I'd love to get going. I hold start dates once the deposit clears, so as soon
> as it's through I'll begin, usually the next working day.

**"Other freelancers don't ask for a deposit."**
> That's fair, everyone works differently. The deposit is what lets me reserve
> the time for you and turn down other work for those weeks.

**"Can the deposit be smaller?"**
> I can do [20%] if we add one more milestone, so the payments stay evenly spread.
*(Only offer this if you're comfortable with it.)*

**"We'll pay the final invoice after launch settles down."**
> The final payment is due on launch, as in the agreement. I'll send the full
> handover the same day it's paid, so your team has everything they need.
